queue.title: Bound the fastmcp dependency before CI resolves into FastMCP 4 and goes red
queue.detail:
FOUND BY TONIGHT'S RESEARCH RUN, and it is the most urgent thing in this queue because it can turn CI red on the next push without anyone touching the code. Read spec-queue/research/2026-09-01.md section '### 1.' for the full evidence.
FACTS IT MEASURED: FastMCP 4.0.0 published to PyPI 2026-08-31T18:20:31Z. This repo declares `fastmcp>=2.0` UNBOUNDED in pyproject.toml:39 and :60 and hub/pyproject.toml:19. CI resolves fresh with no lockfile (.github/workflows/ci.yml:35-36). It installed 4.0.0 in a scratch venv and probed the four APIs hub/hub/mcp_server.py actually uses: all four survive and Literal enums still render -- BUT `FastMCP.get_tools()` is GONE, and that is the introspection layer seven test files sit on. The operator's machine still has 3.4.5, so local green proves nothing about CI.
VERIFY BEFORE ACTING -- the research is a lead, not a verdict. Confirm the pin strings at those exact lines, confirm which tests import or call get_tools(), and confirm 4.0.0 is what a fresh resolve picks today. If any of that does not hold, say so in the log and drop the item rather than 'fixing' something that is not broken.
IF IT HOLDS: apply a defensive UPPER BOUND (e.g. `fastmcp>=2.0,<4`) in all three places. Do not downgrade anything, do not add a lockfile, and do not touch any OTHER unbounded dependency -- `fastapi>=0.110` is an open operator decision (it is in decisions_for_user) and is NOT yours tonight. Add a test that fails when the tool surface's actual APIs stop resolving, so the next major is caught by a named test rather than by CI going red. Run the tool-surface parity tests and `pytest hub/tests/` in the chunk that covers mcp_server.
Then ADD to decisions_for_user: 'fastmcp was bounded to <4 on 2026-09-01 defensively; ratify or widen', with the measured evidence. A bound is reversible in one line, which is why taking it unattended is defensible where changing fastapi would not be.
queue.outcome: DONE, iteration 1, 2026-09-01T01:26+01:00. fastmcp>=2.0 -> fastmcp>=2.0,<4 in all three declarations, plus hub/tests/test_fastmcp_api_contract.py (6 tests) naming every fastmcp API the tool surface stands on. Mutation-checked both ways: removing the bound from one pin, and from all three, each fails a NAMED test with a specific message. 82 passed in the mcp_server chunk, 31 in version+requirement_gate, 3 in tests/test_packaging.py, ruff/black/mypy clean over CI's own paths. ONE CLAIM IN THIS ITEM'S DETAIL WAS WRONG and is corrected in the log: no test anywhere calls get_tools(); the seven files sit on list_tools(), which the research measured as SURVIVING 4.0.0. The research document was right; this queue item's paraphrase of it was not. The action stands on the remaining evidence.

decisions_for_user: NEW 2026-09-01, iteration 10, from row 8 of the sweep: F202 is the one to look at first and it is a two-part decision. GET /projects/{id}/tasks defaults to limit=100, orders by created_at ASCENDING, and answers a bare JSON array with no total, no has_more and no next -- so at 241 tasks the Overview page states '3 agents - 100 tasks' and 'Tasks - 100 total', its nine status chips sum to exactly 100, and a task created seconds ago is not on the board. PART ONE is what the route should answer: keep the array and add a header, wrap it in an envelope (breaking for every existing caller), or drop the default limit for a project-scoped list the way GET /tasks/board already has none. PART TWO is separate and is arguably the sharper problem: mcp_server.py's list_tasks has NO limit or offset parameter at all, so an agent past 100 tasks cannot page even if it knew it should. That half is fixable on its own and probably should be, whatever is decided about part one.

NEW 2026-09-01, iteration 10: F201 asks a rule-shaped question the way F197 did. A Pydantic model_validator on TaskUpdate fires while FastAPI parses the body, so it answers BEFORE the transition machine can -- and an illegal move to 'blocked' comes back 422 'blocked_reason is required' instead of the 409 that names what would be legal, breaching a named scenario in task-lifecycle-governance. The narrow fix is to move that one check behind the machine. THE DECISION is whether the repo wants a standing rule that no request-body validator may refuse something a declared state machine would have refused first -- a sweep for model_validators on request schemas whose subject is also governed by a machine (spec phases, conversation lifecycle, run states) would say how many other places share the ordering.

NEW 2026-09-01, iteration 10: F203 is a build-or-decline, not a bug. task_transitions is append-only, carries actor_kind/actor_agent/run_id/origin/policy_digest, has a history_for() reader, and NO route or MCP tool exposes it -- the drives have had to open sqlite to say anything about who moved a task. Either add GET /tasks/{id}/transitions (small, and it would have shortened F154 and F167 considerably), or decide the history is an internal audit trail and say so where the module claims it is 'worth reading'.

NEW 2026-09-01, iteration 9, from row 7 of the sweep: F196 and F198 are two halves of one question the operator should settle -- SHOULD PATCH /queue/settings EXIST AT ALL? It writes four columns that PUT /projects/{id}/settings already owns, with a weaker contract on both ends: no upper bound (so it can store a value that makes the settings page 500 on read AND on write, F196) and non-partial PATCH semantics (so it silently reverts agent_budget and allow_agent_jobs, F198). The UI never calls it. The three options are: delete it and let the project settings route own these columns; keep it and make it derive its bounds and its optionality from ProjectSettings the way ProjectSettingsUpdate already does; or keep it as-is and document it as an expert API. The narrow fixes (add le=1000; make the two defaulted fields Optional and merge) are safe and queueable either way, and separately projects.py:463 should move inside its own try so a stored value out of range cannot wedge the route that would repair it.

NEW 2026-09-01, iteration 9: F197 asks a rule-shaped question, not a component-shaped one. ProjectSettingsPanel renders a loading skeleton whenever its query has no data and reads only its MUTATIONS' errors, so a 500, a dropped connection and an expired key all look like 'still loading', forever. THE DECISION is whether the repo wants a standing rule that a panel gated on a query's data must render that query's error state -- a sweep for React Query results used without their `error` would say how many other panels have the same gap. F196 is only the fastest way to reach it.

NEW 2026-09-01, iteration 8, from row 6 of the sweep: F193 makes the rail's two views disagree about which conversations exist -- an open conversation whose agent was archived is dropped by AgentTree (it iterates the roster) and listed by RecencyView (it iterates the conversations). THE DECISION is not the display bug, which is a filter either way, but what archiving an agent should MEAN for the threads it owns: leave them open and orphaned (today), archive them with the agent, or refuse the archive while any thread is open -- the same three-way choice the product already made explicitly for archiving a CONVERSATION with a live run, where it refuses and says why. Whichever is chosen, App.tsx:371-374's bare 'Agent unavailable.' should say the agent is archived and that unarchiving is one click; the product already owns that sentence one route away.

NEW 2026-09-01, iteration 8: F195 found a dead cwd parameter -- the conversation titler spawns claude -p in the HUB PROCESS's working directory, not the project's, proven with a positive control against a planted CLAUDE.md. The narrow fix is threading ProjectWorkspace's path through two call sites and is queueable either way.
